Reference: Ali and Lin (2013)

Model Setting

Why do people vote when no single vote is pivotal? The paper combines two motives that had been modelled separately. Ethical citizens are group rule-utilitarians in the sense of Harsanyi (1980), Coate and Conlin (2004) and Feddersen and Sandroni (2006): they follow the voting rule that would maximize the welfare of their group if all ethical members followed it. Pragmatists do not care about the rule; they vote only because voting is observed by others and they wish to be perceived as ethical. Social pressure is therefore not a reduced-form reward for voting: the esteem attached to voting and the stigma attached to abstaining are posterior beliefs, computed by Bayes' rule from the equilibrium participation rates of the two types. A political equilibrium is a profile of cost cutoffs in which the ethical cutoffs of the two groups are mutually consistent given the behaviour of pragmatists, and the pragmatists' cutoffs are best responses in the signaling game given the ethical cutoffs.

The main findings are as follows. A political equilibrium exists and is unique, and is characterized by one equation. Because pragmatists imitate ethical citizens, all citizens vote more when the election is more important, when it is expected to be closer and when voting costs fall, so the competitive predictions of ethical voter models survive even if many voters are not intrinsically motivated. Stronger social incentives (greater observability of voting, larger rewards or sanctions) raise the turnout of pragmatists and average turnout but lower the turnout of ethical citizens, a crowding out of intrinsic by extrinsic motivation. Social pressure never produces overvoting: pragmatists vote only at costs at which ethical citizens also vote. Signaling alone cannot generate turnout: as the share of ethical citizens vanishes, turnout vanishes. With asymmetric groups, the group with stronger social incentives has less active ethical citizens but higher average turnout and a higher probability of winning. Extensions show that the detection of lies about voting and community knowledge of voting costs both raise turnout, which speaks to higher turnout in tightly knit communities, and that candidates pander to the group that is better mobilized. The paper is purely theoretical; it motivates the model with the field experiment of Gerber, Green and Larimer (2008), in which telling voters that their neighbours would learn whether they voted raised turnout from 29.7 percent to 37.8 percent, and with Funk (2010), who finds that optional postal voting in Switzerland lowered voting costs without raising aggregate turnout and reduced turnout in small communities, where voting in person is most visible.

A continuum of citizens belongs to one of two groups, G∈{1,2}G\in\{1,2\}G∈{1,2}; members of group 1 prefer alternative 1 and members of group 2 prefer alternative 2, and the winner is decided by majority rule. Each citizen iii either votes for the alternative of her group (ai=1a_i=1ai​=1) or abstains (ai=0a_i=0ai​=0). Voting costs cic_ici​ are distributed according to a cdf FFF whose pdf fff is continuous and strictly positive on [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞). The fraction of citizens in group 1, kkk, is uncertain: it follows a symmetric beta distribution on [0,1][0,1][0,1] with parameter α\alphaα, which is uniform for α=1\alpha=1α=1 and single-peaked around 1/21/21/2 for α>1\alpha>1α>1. It is convenient to work with the ratio of group sizes x=k/(1−k)x=k/(1-k)x=k/(1−k), whose density is:

h(x,α)=xα−1(1+x)2αB(α,α)(1)h(x,\alpha)=\frac{x^{\alpha-1}}{(1+x)^{2\alpha}B(\alpha,\alpha)} \tag{1}h(x,α)=(1+x)2αB(α,α)xα−1​(1)

where B(α,α)B(\alpha,\alpha)B(α,α) is the beta function and H(x)H(x)H(x) denotes the cdf of xxx. The payoff induces a threshold rule: a pragmatist in group GGG votes if and only if ci≤c^Gc_i\leq\hat{c}_Gci​≤c^G​. Ethical Citizens and the Consistent Rule

Each citizen believes that the collective gain to her group is www when its preferred alternative wins; www is the importance of the election. Ethical citizens also want aggregate voting costs to be low. Group 2 wins when its votes exceed those of group 1, that is, when the size ratio xxx is below the ratio of the group turnout rates. The welfare perceived by the ethical citizens of each group is therefore:

The ethical rule is a threshold rule, because a given turnout is achieved at the lowest cost by having the lowest-cost citizens vote. A profile (c1∗,c2∗)\left(c^*_1,c^*_2\right)(c1∗​,c2∗​) is a Consistent Ethical Response to (c^1,c^2)\left(\hat{c}_1,\hat{c}_2\right)(c^1​,c^2​) if, for every group GGG, the cutoff cG∗c^*_GcG∗​ maximizes VGV_GVG​ over all c>0c>0c>0, holding fixed the cutoff c−G∗c^*_{-G}c−G∗​ of the other group and the cutoffs of pragmatists. The welfare function counts the voting costs of pragmatists but not their signaling payoffs: ethical citizens do not account for the welfare that pragmatists derive from image. Pragmatists are assumed to vote for the alternative of their group, either because once the cost is sunk a negligible pivot probability makes this strictly optimal, or because voting for the inferior alternative carries a psychological cost.

A political equilibrium is a profile {(c1∗,c2∗),(c^1,c^2)}\left\{\left(c^*_1,c^*_2\right),\left(\hat{c}_1,\hat{c}_2\right)\right\}{(c1∗​,c2∗​),(c^1​,c^2​)} such that the first pair is a Consistent Ethical Response to the second pair, and each element of the second pair is a Pragmatic Best Response to the corresponding ethical cutoff. Ethical and pragmatic citizens thus respond to each other, in opposite directions: pragmatists follow ethical citizens, while ethical citizens compensate for pragmatists.

Property 2 (social incentives). An increase in λ\lambdaλ decreases the participation rate of ethical citizens but increases that of pragmatists and the average participation rate. Differentiating the indifference condition gives:

Hence cG∗c^*_GcG∗​ falls, and for the equilibrium condition to keep holding, the turnout rate qF(cG∗)+(1−q)F(P(cG∗))qF\left(c^*_G\right)+(1-q)F\left(P\left(c^*_G\right)\right)qF(cG∗​)+(1−q)F(P(cG∗​)) must rise, which requires more voting by pragmatists. Ethical citizens compensate less for pragmatists when pragmatists vote more. This is a crowding out of intrinsic by extrinsic motivation: voters become more extrinsically motivated on average and abstainers more intrinsically motivated. The property rationalizes the social pressure experiment of Gerber, Green and Larimer (2008) and the postal voting evidence of Funk (2010) as changes in λ\lambdaλ.

Property 3 (no overvoting). For all values of λ\lambdaλ, pragmatists vote only at costs at which ethical citizens also vote, c^G<cG∗\hat{c}_G<c^*_Gc^G​<cG∗​. By the indifference condition, c^G>0\hat{c}_G>0c^G​>0 if and only if S(c^G,cG∗)>0S\left(\hat{c}_G,c^*_G\right)>0S(c^G​,cG∗​)>0, which holds if and only if F(c^G)<F(cG∗)F\left(\hat{c}_G\right)<F\left(c^*_G\right)F(c^G​)<F(cG∗​). If pragmatists voted more than ethical citizens, abstention would be the better signal and no pragmatist would pay to vote. As λ→∞\lambda\rightarrow\inftyλ→∞ the pragmatist cutoff approaches the ethical cutoff from below and the image gap dissolves. This is the main welfare remark of the paper: unlike in Benabou and Tirole (2006) or Daughety and Reinganum (2010), where social pressure can push prosocial behaviour above the efficient level, here esteem can never induce turnout beyond what the ethical rule of the group prescribes.

Property 4 (signaling alone is not enough). As q→0q\rightarrow0q→0, the participation rate of ethical citizens converges to full participation, F(cG∗)→1F\left(c^*_G\right)\rightarrow1F(cG∗​)→1, but overall turnout vanishes. Along a sequence qn→0q_n\rightarrow0qn​→0 with cutoffs cG,n∗c^*_{G,n}cG,n∗​ and c^G,n\hat{c}_{G,n}c^G,n​, the gain in image is at most the image of a voter, which the indifference condition bounds by:

c^G,nF(c^G,n)<λqn1−qn(16)\hat{c}_{G,n}F\left(\hat{c}_{G,n}\right)<\frac{\lambda q_n}{1-q_n} \tag{16}c^G,n​F(c^G,n​)<1−qn​λqn​​(16)

so c^G,n→0\hat{c}_{G,n}\rightarrow0c^G,n​→0 and aggregate turnout, which is asymptotically that of pragmatists, vanishes; the equilibrium condition can then hold only if cG,n∗→∞c^*_{G,n}\rightarrow\inftycG,n∗​→∞. When almost nobody is ethical, voting cannot shift beliefs much, as with reputation effects that disappear when the prior on the commitment type vanishes at a fixed discount factor. Evidence of social incentives therefore implies a substantial share of both types.

The proofs of the next two properties rest on an equation of the online appendix that is the analogue of the equality of cutoff times turnout across groups, and they are only sketched in the published appendix.

Property 5. If w2>w1w_2>w_1w2​>w1​, or if F1F_1F1​ first-order stochastically dominates F2F_2F2​, the participation rates of both ethical citizens and pragmatists are higher in group 2, which therefore wins with higher probability. The group that cares more or finds voting cheaper has a higher ethical cutoff, and its pragmatists follow because PPP is increasing. Subsidizing the turnout of one group, or adding ballot propositions that matter more to it, yields a political gain.

Property 6. If λ1<λ2\lambda_1<\lambda_2λ1​<λ2​, then P2(c)>P1(c)P_2(c)>P_1(c)P2​(c)>P1​(c) for every ccc by Property 2, and in equilibrium c1∗>c2∗c^*_1>c^*_2c1∗​>c2∗​: ethical citizens in group 2 participate less than those in group 1. Nevertheless average participation is higher in group 2, which has a higher probability of winning. This resembles an underdog effect: the ethical citizens of the group with weaker social incentives vote more to compensate for the rest of their group, but not enough to offset the other group's aggregate turnout. The image gap between voters and abstainers is larger in group 1, and voters of group 2 are more likely to be motivated by social rewards.

Extension: Votes and Lies

Why vote if one can simply claim to have voted? Suppose that after the decision a perfectly informative signal of the action is revealed to others with probability sss, and that before this each citizen sends a message about her choice, which need not be truthful. Ethical citizens follow the ethical rule and report truthfully. Let c~G\tilde{c}_Gc~G​ be the cutoff of pragmatists and μG\mu_GμG​ the fraction of pragmatists that abstain and falsely claim to vote. where the first term applies when hard information proves that she voted and the second relies on cheap talk alone. A citizen who abstains and admits it has the image:

because a detected lie reveals a pragmatist. The Pragmatic Best Response is now a pair (c~G,μG)\left(\tilde{c}_G,\mu_G\right)(c~G​,μG​) such that pragmatists with cost below c~G\tilde{c}_Gc~G​ vote and say so, those above abstain and a fraction μG\mu_GμG​ of all pragmatists lies, the cutoff equals λ\lambdaλ times the difference between the voter's image and the truthful abstainer's image, and, if μG>0\mu_G>0μG​>0, the truthful and the lying abstainer have the same image. Some abstaining pragmatists must admit abstention, since otherwise that message would be sent only by ethical citizens and would earn the highest esteem; liars therefore randomize. With s=0s=0s=0 no pragmatist votes, and the fraction that claims to vote equals the fraction of ethical citizens that votes, so that image does not depend on the message. This is the model's account of the overreporting of voting in surveys.

Theorem 2. There is a unique political equilibrium, in which for every group GGG:

With asymmetric monitoring, the better monitored group is more likely to win. The proof is in the online appendix.

Extension: Observable Voting Costs

In communities with frequent interaction, others may know how costly voting is for a given person. Suppose each individual believes that with probability p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1]p∈[0,1] others in her community know her cost realization. A simple threshold equilibrium for pragmatists cannot exist, because the image from voting would be discontinuous at the threshold, so pragmatists mix. Let μc\mu^cμc be the probability that a pragmatist with cost ccc votes, μ^=∫0∞μcdF\hat{\mu}=\int_0^{\infty}\mu^cdFμ^​=∫0∞​μcdF the participation rate of all pragmatists in the group, and μ∗=F(c∗)\mu^*=F\left(c^*\right)μ∗=F(c∗) that of ethical citizens. Theorem 3. For every p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1]p∈[0,1] there is a unique political equilibrium, in which for every group GGG:

cG∗(qμG∗+(1−q)μ^)=21−2αwB(α,α)(24)c^*_G\left(q\mu^*_G+(1-q)\hat{\mu}\right)=\frac{2^{1-2\alpha}w}{B(\alpha,\alpha)} \tag{24}cG∗​(qμG∗​+(1−q)μ^​)=B(α,α)21−2αw​(24)

Pragmatists with cost below λq\lambda qλq vote with probability one and obtain exactly the prior image qqq: voting is not rewarded, but abstaining would be punished with an image of zero. At costs between λq\lambda qλq and c∗c^*c∗ the prior image is not worth the cost, yet abstaining with probability one is not an equilibrium either, since a voter would then be taken for ethical; pragmatists randomize so that the reward λq/(q+(1−q)μc)\lambda q/\left(q+(1-q)\mu^c\right)λq/(q+(1−q)μc) equals the cost, and the probability of voting falls with the cost. Above c∗c^*c∗ no pragmatist votes. Observable costs can remove the gap between the two types altogether. Let c†c^{\dagger}c† be the unique solution of cF(c)=21−2αw/B(α,α)cF(c)=2^{1-2\alpha}w/B(\alpha,\alpha)cF(c)=21−2αw/B(α,α), the ethical cutoff when everyone behaves as an ethical citizen. If p>0p>0p>0 and λpq>c†\lambda pq>c^{\dagger}λpq>c†, then in the unique political equilibrium all pragmatists vote exactly as ethical citizens do. In communities where neighbours know each other's circumstances, extrinsic incentives are powerful, and they work through the stigma of abstaining, not the honor of voting.

Other Extensions

Two further extensions are only summarized in the paper, with details in the online appendix. Under naive ethics, each ethical citizen believes that every citizen is ethical and so does not compensate for pragmatists; a naive political equilibrium exists and is unique, has lower turnout than the benchmark, and has similar comparative statics. With a continuum of types, individuals value following the ethical rule to different degrees, measured by an ethical coefficient. There must then be a group of pure ethical citizens with a strict incentive to follow the rule, since otherwise a Consistent Ethical Response fails to exist; other citizens care about the extent to which they are seen as pure ethical citizens, and a unique political equilibrium continues to exist.

w1(p1,p2)w2(p1,p2)=(1κ)(u(12)−u(12+x)u(12−x)−u(12))(26)\frac{w_1\left(p_1,p_2\right)}{w_2\left(p_1,p_2\right)}=\left(\frac{1}{\kappa}\right)\left(\frac{u\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)-u\left(\frac{1}{2}+x\right)}{u\left(\frac{1}{2}-x\right)-u\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}\right) \tag{26}w2​(p1​,p2​)w1​(p1​,p2​)​=(κ1​)(u(21​−x)−u(21​)u(21​)−u(21​+x)​)(26)

Theorem 4 (office motivation). In the unique equilibrium both candidates choose the same platform, all citizens abstain and each candidate wins with equal probability. With asymmetric responsiveness:

p1=p2={32if κ<κx32+xif κ>κx(27)p_1=p_2= \begin{cases} \frac{3}{2} & \text{if } \kappa<\kappa_x\\ \frac{3}{2}+x & \text{if } \kappa>\kappa_x \end{cases} \tag{27}p1​=p2​={23​23​+x​if κ<κx​if κ>κx​​(27)

With asymmetric social incentives, there exist κˉ>1\bar{\kappa}>1κˉ>1 and λ‾\underline{\lambda}λ​ such that if κx<κˉ\kappa_x<\bar{\kappa}κx​<κˉ and λ2>λ‾\lambda_2>\underline{\lambda}λ2​>λ​, the unique platform is 32+x\frac{3}{2}+x23​+x. The logic is that a candidate who wins with probability below one half can copy the opponent, eliminate turnout and split the election, so the equilibrium platform must be one that no other platform defeats with probability above one half. Turnout is zero on the path, yet the threat of off-path turnout disciplines platforms, which reflect the intensity and not only the ordering of preferences. Since κx→1\kappa_x\rightarrow1κx​→1 as x→0x\rightarrow0x→0, any asymmetry would induce some pandering in a continuous policy space. Office-motivated candidates gain nothing from investing in social incentives.

Theorem 5 (policy motivation). Candidate GGG has ideal policy GGG and payoff v(∣p−G∣)v\left(|p-G|\right)v(∣p−G∣) from policy ppp, with vvv smooth, strictly decreasing and strictly concave. Define:

vx=v(12−x)−v(12+x)v(12)−v(12+x)>1(28)v_x=\frac{v\left(\frac{1}{2}-x\right)-v\left(\frac{1}{2}+x\right)}{v\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)-v\left(\frac{1}{2}+x\right)}>1 \tag{28}vx​=v(21​)−v(21​+x)v(21​−x)−v(21​+x)​>1(28)

Policy-motivated candidates choose different platforms in the unique equilibrium, either (32−x,32+x)\left(\frac{3}{2}-x,\frac{3}{2}+x\right)(23​−x,23​+x) or (32,32+x)\left(\frac{3}{2},\frac{3}{2}+x\right)(23​,23​+x), so citizens vote on the equilibrium path. Under asymmetric responsiveness, there exist vˉ>1\bar{v}>1vˉ>1 and κˉ\bar{\kappa}κˉ such that the second pair is the unique equilibrium if κ>κˉ\kappa>\bar{\kappa}κ>κˉ and vx<vˉv_x<\bar{v}vx​<vˉ. Under asymmetric social incentives, there exist vˉ>1\bar{v}>1vˉ>1, κˉ>1\bar{\kappa}>1κˉ>1 and λ‾\underline{\lambda}λ​ such that it is the unique equilibrium if vx<vˉv_x<\bar{v}vx​<vˉ, κx<κˉ\kappa_x<\bar{\kappa}κx​<κˉ and λ2>λ‾\lambda_2>\underline{\lambda}λ2​>λ​. The probability that candidate 2 wins is increasing in κ\kappaκ and in λ2\lambda_2λ2​. Candidate 1 moves to the centre because this makes the election relatively less important to group 2 than to group 1 and so raises his winning probability, even though no member of group 2 votes for him. Unlike an office-motivated candidate, a policy-motivated candidate wants to strengthen social incentives in the group that favours him, which is why political elites invest in mobilization: it changes both who wins and which platforms are offered. The proofs of both theorems are in the online appendix.

Linearity in the posterior makes the model tractable: only the difference between the image of a voter and the image of an abstainer matters for the decision, and the level of image cancels. This equation makes the stakes of the election endogenous in the electoral application. Group GGG has its ideal point at the location G∈{1,2}G\in\{1,2\}G∈{1,2}; a policy ppp gives it the collective payoff κGu(∣p−G∣)\kappa_Gu\left(|p-G|\right)κG​u(∣p−G∣), where ∣p−G∣|p-G|∣p−G∣ is the distance from the ideal point, uuu is strictly decreasing and strictly concave, and κG>0\kappa_G>0κG​>0 scales how much the group cares about policy. The absolute value appears because the group simply supports whichever platform is closer to its ideal point.

Office-motivated candidates must each win with probability one half in equilibrium, since a candidate with a lower chance can copy the opponent, which sets wG=0w_G=0wG​=0, eliminates turnout and splits the election.
